title: Lips
description: Conditions affecting the vermilion, the angles of the mouth, and the perioral skin.

problems.description: Red, sore, cracked skin at the corners of the mouth. Often a gold crust by morning. Worse with drooling, dentures, or anaemia.
problems.etiology:
A combined infection at the corners of the mouth. Three usual organisms: **Staphylococcus aureus, β-haemolytic streptococci, and Candida** [1]. The bugs don't get there on their own — they exploit a moist, macerated angle of the mouth that's been set up by something else.

The two big setups:

- **Local**: trauma, drooling, an ill-fitting denture with reduced occlusal vertical dimension that lets the upper lip fold into the lower [1].
- **Systemic**: iron deficiency and vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia [1]. Iron-deficiency anaemia in particular is a well-recognised cause [2], and angular cheilitis is one of the textbook signs of it [3].

What happens is moisture pools in the fold, the skin macerates, and the bug mix moves in. Without fixing the underlying setup, treatment alone runs out of steam [1].
problems.presentation:
What you'll see at the corners:

- Red, cracked, macerated skin — often with a gold crust [1].
- Usually bilateral when the cause is denture or systemic; can be unilateral with local trauma.
- Sore but not severely painful. Often splits when the patient yawns or eats.

Look in the rest of the mouth too — angular cheilitis travels with other candidal and denture problems. Denture stomatitis on the palate, papillary hyperplasia under the upper denture, and a smooth red tongue are commonly there alongside [1].
problems.results:
- **Swab from the commissure**: typically grows the staph–strep–Candida mix [1]; in denture-associated cases it often grows S. aureus, sensitive to fusidic acid [4]. Sensitivities steer the topical choice.
- **FBC and haematinics**: iron, ferritin, B12, folate [1]. Microcytic hypochromic picture points hard at iron deficiency [3].
- **Denture assessment**: occlusal vertical dimension, fit, hygiene, age. An overclosed denture sets up the fold [1].
- **Blood glucose** if there's coexisting candidosis — diabetes predisposes to candida.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing that distinguishes angular cheilitis from look-alikes: **it's at the angles of the mouth and almost always has a candidal component.**

Compare to:

- **Cold sore**: vesicles on the vermilion or skin near the lip with a tingling prodrome — not strictly at the angle.
- **Contact dermatitis**: itchy, more diffuse, history of new lipstick / toothpaste / chewing gum.
- **Orofacial granulomatosis**: persistent firm lip swelling and cobblestone buccal mucosa; angular cheilitis can develop on top [5].

The bilateral pattern, the gold crust, and the link to a denture or anaemia are the giveaways.
problems.treatment:
Two arms run in parallel — clear the infection, fix the cause [1].

**Topical antifungal/antibacterial:**

- **Miconazole cream** is first-line — covers all three usual organisms (strep, staph, Candida) [1, 6]. Apply qds [6].
- **If swab shows S. aureus**, fusidic acid cream is appropriate [4].
- **Mupirocin to the anterior nares** if Staph keeps coming back — clears the nasal reservoir [1].
- Treat for at least 10 days **after** the lesion looks resolved. Short courses relapse [1].

**Underlying cause:**

- Replace or rebase the denture if the vertical dimension is wrong [1].
- Correct anaemia — iron, B12, or folate replacement under the GP [1].
- Treat coexisting denture stomatitis: leave dentures out at night, soak in chlorhexidine, miconazole gel to the fitting surface.

**Watch-out**: miconazole interacts with warfarin (raises INR), antidiabetics, antiepileptics, and a few other drug classes [7]. Check the medical history before prescribing.
problems.prognosis:
- Treat both arms (infection + cause) → resolves in 1–2 weeks and stays resolved [1].
- Treat the infection only → comes back. The setup is still there [1].
- Keeps recurring without an obvious local cause → think systemic. Anaemia, diabetes, immunosuppression [2, 3].

**Rule of thumb**: angular cheilitis on a denture wearer is a denture problem until proven otherwise. Recurrent bilateral angular cheilitis without dentures deserves bloods.

citations.quote: A combined staphylococcal, β-haemolytic streptococci, and candidal infection, involving the tissues at the angle of the mouth (Fig. 11.1). Aetiology is multifactorial with local and systemic precipitating factors, e.g. trauma, inadequate vertical dimension of denture, iron deficiency, and vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia. Therefore, FBC and haematinics should be investigated. Clinically, red, cracked, macerated skin at angles of the mouth, often with a gold crust. Rx: miconazole cream, which is active against all three infecting organisms. Rx needs to be prolonged, up to 10 days after resolution of clinical lesion, and carried out in conjunction with elimination of any underlying factors. Mupirocin cream applied to the anterior nares helps eradicate sources of Staphylococcus aureus.

Candidosis (…… Oral candidosis (candidiasis), p. 438) may be precipitated or exacerbated by anaemia, particularly iron deficiency, and angular cheilitis is a well-recognized association. The sore, clinically normal tongue (burning tongue) is sometimes a manifestation or even precursor of anaemia.

These are notoriously unreliable, but may include general fatigue, heart failure, angina on effort, pallor (look at conjunctivae and palmar creases, but unreliable), brittle nails &/or spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), oral discomfort &/or ulceration, glossitis, and classically angular cheilitis.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 7182 (signs of iron-deficiency anaemia)

citations.quote: In this case, a swab was taken from the commissure and surrounding skin. Culture revealed Staphylococcus aureus, which was sensitive to fusidic acid.

Lip swelling affects the majority of patients, with each episode lasting days to weeks. Over time, the lips may become firm and persistently swollen. The perioral skin may become red, dry, itchy or cracked, with some patients developing angular cheilitis.
citations.source: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving · paragraph 7906 (orofacial granulomatosis)

citations.quote: This is a useful drug, particularly in management of angular cheilitis, as it is active against streptococci, staphylococci, and Candida. Miconazole oral gel 24mg/mL is of use in chronic mucocutaneous and chronic hyperplastic candidosis. Dose: 2.5mL qds 20mg/g gel. Apply a pea-sized amount after food qds. Can be applied to dentures also. Miconazole cream is used topically for angular cheilitis.

There are recognized potentially serious interactions between miconazole, fluconazole, and related drugs and antibacterials, anticoagulants, antidiabetics, antiepileptics, antihistamines, anxiolytics, cisapride, ciclosporin, and theophylline. Check what your patient is currently taking.

problems.description: Recurring cluster of tiny blisters on the vermilion or the skin just above it. Burning and tingling before the blisters appear. Heals within 1–2 weeks then comes back.
problems.etiology:
The virus responsible is herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). The reason labialis can keep recurring is that HSV-1 doesn't clear after the primary infection — it travels back along sensory axons to the trigeminal or geniculate ganglion and stays there as a latent infection [1]. A viral latency gene and the cell-mediated immune response keep the balance between latency and reactivation [2].

When the balance tips toward reactivation, the virus travels back down the nerve to the skin or mucosa at the mucocutaneous junction of the lip. The reason antibodies don't prevent recurrences is that for most of its life cycle the virus is intracellular, putting it out of reach of the humoral response [2].

Environmental triggers for reactivation include ultraviolet light, illness, and stress [2]. Trauma — for example, removal of a wisdom tooth — and immunosuppression are also recognised precipitants [3].
problems.presentation:
The patient usually knows it's coming before you can see anything. The prodrome is a burning or tingling sensation at the site, lasting up to 24 hours [3]. Then:

- Small vesicles appear at the vermilion border or the skin immediately above or below it [3].
- Vesicles rupture quickly, leaving shallow painful erosions, which crust over.
- Confined to one branch of the trigeminal nerve — usually recurs on the same patch of lip [3].
- Recurrences are seen in up to 30% of patients who have had a primary HSV infection [3].
problems.results:
Herpes labialis is a clinical diagnosis. Special investigations are rarely needed in primary care.

- If there is doubt, viral swab from the lesion base can confirm HSV by PCR.
- The prodrome + vesiculation + mucocutaneous junction site + previous history of recurrences is the defining pattern [2, 3].
- Labial recurrences are painful and unpleasant but relatively readily treated because there is often a characteristic prodromal sensation of burning or itching and the vesicles are easily seen [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing that sets herpes labialis apart:

- **Site**: mucocutaneous junction of the lip — not strictly at the angle (angular cheilitis), not diffusely across the mucosa (primary HSV stomatitis).
- **Prodrome**: burning or tingling reliably precedes the vesicles [3]. Angular cheilitis has no prodrome; mucocele has no pain at all.
- **Recurrence pattern**: same site, same nerve territory, same trigger pattern [3].
- **Erythema multiforme connection**: recurrent HSV is a common trigger for erythema multiforme — a cold sore 1–2 weeks before the onset of lip crusting and oral erosions raises this possibility [5].
problems.treatment:
The goal is to start treatment in the prodrome, before vesicles form — that's when antivirals make the most difference [4].

- **Aciclovir 5% cream**: apply to the site of prodromal or early lesion 4-hourly for 5 days [6].
- **Penciclovir 1% cream**: apply 2-hourly for 4 days — also prescribable for herpes labialis [7].
- Both are most effective in the prodromal or early vesicular stage [3, 6]. Started late, they shorten duration but can't abort the episode.
- **Systemic aciclovir** (400mg PO five times daily for 5 days) [6] should be considered in the immunocompromised or for frequent recurrences [3].
- Sun block on the lips reduces UV-triggered recurrences.
problems.prognosis:
- Each episode is self-limiting, resolving in about 1–2 weeks without treatment.
- Up to 30% of people who acquire HSV go on to have recurrent cold sores [8]; many suffer only occasional lesions, and frequency tends to decrease with age.
- In immunocompromised patients, recurrences can be more severe and more frequent — systemic antivirals are the appropriate response [3].
- There is no cure. Latent infection in the ganglion persists for life [2].

citations.quote: During infection, HSV is transported back along axons of sensory nerves to their nuclei. There, the neurones are infected but do not die, and the virus becomes latent – that is, virus persists but no infectious virions are produced.

A viral latency gene and the cell-mediated immune response contribute to the balance between latency and reactivation. If infection is reactivated, the virus travels down the nerve to cause a localized recurrent infection of the mucosa or skin – a cold sore. Because the virus is intracellular for most of this life cycle, antibodies of the humoral immune response are not effective in preventing recurrences. Environmental triggers for cold sores include ultraviolet light, illness and stress.

These are seen in up to 30% of patients affecting the mucocutaneous junction of the lips (herpes labialis, cold sore) and result from reactivation of the 1° infection which is believed to lie dormant in the dorsal root, and autonomic or cranial nerve ganglia (trigeminal or geniculate). Precipitating factors include trauma, e.g. during removal of 8 and immunosuppression and, less commonly, exposure to sunlight, stress, and febrile illness. Usually recurs on area of distribution supplied by one branch of the trigeminal nerve. Prodromal phase (burning/tingling) over 24h is followed by vesiculation and pain. Lesions may respond to 1% penciclovir or aciclovir 5% cream if used in the prodromal stage. Should consider systemic aciclovir (…… Aciclovir, p. 612) in the immunosuppressed or frequent recurrences.

Labial recurrences are painful and unpleasant but relatively readily treated because there is often a characteristic prodromal sensation of burning or itching and the vesicles are easily seen. Early treatment is, therefore, possible, and antiviral drugs can be very effective. Topical preparations of 5% aciclovir are available without prescription.

If the patient has had recurrent HSV infection, usually in the form of herpes labialis, then the present ulcers could not have been caused by a primary herpetic infection. Recurrent herpetic infection is sometimes a trigger for attacks of erythema multiforme and a cold sore 1–2 weeks before onset would raise this possibility.

Active against herpes simplex and zoster; relatively non-toxic and can be given systemically or topically. Dose: herpes labialis: apply 5% aciclovir cream to site of prodromal or early lesion 4-hourly for 5 days; herpetic stomatitis: 200mg PO (400mg in immunocompromised) five times daily for 5 days; herpes zoster: 800mg PO five times daily for 7 days.
Penciclovir as a 1% cream applied 2-hourly for 4 days is prescribable according to the DPF for herpes labialis.

Between 15 and 30% of individuals who come into contact with the virus develop recurrent infection. It is not clear whether those who suffer a symptomatic primary infection such as gingivostomatitis have an increased risk. Although this percentage seems high, many patients with recurrent herpes infection suffer only very occasional lesions.

problems.description: A smooth, soft, painless fluid-filled lump on the inner surface of the lower lip that appeared after lip-biting or minor trauma. Bluish, translucent. Recurs if not fully removed.
problems.etiology:
The mechanism is simple: a minor salivary duct gets traumatised — most often by a bite — and saliva leaks out of the duct into the surrounding connective tissue. The spilled saliva doesn't drain away; instead it pools and is walled off by compressed connective tissue, forming a pseudocyst [1].

The reason mucoceles mostly appear on the lower lip is anatomy: the minor salivary gland ducts of the lower lip are exposed to biting trauma far more than those on the upper lip [1]. This matters clinically — a similar-looking swelling on the upper lip is much more likely to be a minor salivary gland tumour and should be treated with more suspicion [1, 2].

A minority are true mucous retention cysts rather than extravasation pseudocysts [1], but the clinical distinction rarely changes management.
problems.presentation:
- Smooth, soft, dome-shaped swelling on the inner surface of the lower lip, typically 5–10 mm in diameter.
- Bluish or translucent in colour when superficial; flesh-coloured if it lies deeper in the tissue.
- Painless. The patient often presents because they've noticed the lump or keep biting it.
- History of repeated trauma or biting at the site is common.
- May have burst spontaneously before the appointment, leaving a flat, mildly sore area — and then re-formed.
problems.results:
Mucocele is a clinical diagnosis based on site, appearance, and history.

- **Aspiration**: aspirating a thin, clear-to-slightly-viscous fluid (saliva) confirms the diagnosis and differentiates it from a vascular lesion (which would aspirate blood).
- No imaging is required for a straightforward lower-lip mucocele.
- **Histology** after excision is standard practice and confirms the mucous extravasation pattern — compressed connective tissue wall without a true epithelial lining.
- Any swelling on the **upper lip** warrants biopsy and histology rather than clinical assumption: >50% of upper lip minor salivary gland tumours are malignant [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key distinguishing features:

- **Lower lip, inner surface**: this is the signature site. Upper lip swellings are a red flag for salivary tumour [1, 2].
- **Fluctuant and translucent**: unlike a fibrous epulis or fibroma, which are firm and opaque.
- **Bursts and recurs**: spontaneous rupture followed by re-accumulation is almost pathognomonic of mucocele.
- Unlike a ranula (which is a mucocele of the floor of the mouth arising from the sublingual gland [3]), labial mucoceles are superficial and straightforwardly excised.
problems.treatment:
Excision of the mucocele together with the associated damaged minor salivary gland and duct [1]. The reason the gland must come out with the cyst is that leaving it behind almost guarantees recurrence — the damaged duct continues to leak.

- Performed under local anaesthesia in primary care or a minor surgery setting.
- Send the specimen for histology — confirms diagnosis and excludes an unexpected tumour.
- Marsupialisation alone is not recommended; the recurrence rate is high.
- For an **upper lip** swelling: do not assume mucocele. Refer for specialist assessment — the majority of minor salivary gland tumours at this site are malignant [2].
problems.prognosis:
- Excision with the associated gland: low recurrence rate.
- Excision of the cyst alone without the gland: high likelihood of recurrence.
- Natural history without treatment: some smaller mucoceles rupture and resolve spontaneously but most recur. Repeated biting of a persisting mucocele keeps the cycle going.

citations.quote: These are usually mucous extravasation cysts, where saliva leaks from a traumatized duct and pools, creating a compressed connective tissue capsule. Rarely, they are mucous retention cysts. They mostly affect the lower lip—similar swellings in the upper lip are often minor salivary gland tumours (…… Salivary gland tumours, p. 513). Rx: excision with associated damaged glands and duct.

>50% of tumours are malignant (mostly adenoid cystic) and require extensive surgery and reconstruction similar to floor of mouth cancer. Beware the 'mucocele' of the upper lip—it is almost certainly a tumour.

These are mucoceles of the floor of the mouth, arising from the sublingual gland. They tend to recur if marsupialized. A plunging ranula crosses deep to the mylohyoid and appears as a neck and floor of mouth swelling. Rx: excision of cyst and associated sublingual gland; the submandibular gland may have to be excised if the duct is damaged.

problems.description: Painless, non-healing ulcer or thickened white patch on the lower lip vermilion. History of long-term sun exposure. Present for more than 3 weeks.
problems.conditionName: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip
problems.etiology:
The main aetiological factor in cancer of the lip is exposure to sunlight — the same mechanism as skin cancer [1]. The risk doubles every 250 miles nearer the equator, which is the clearest statement of the dose-response relationship [1]. Actinic cheilitis — sun damage to the lower lip causing excessive keratin production and increased mitotic activity in the basal layer — is the recognised premalignant precursor [2].

The lower lip is almost exclusively affected because it receives direct ultraviolet radiation; the upper lip is shaded by the philtrum. This origin-specific pattern distinguishes lip SCC from intraoral SCC, which is driven more by tobacco and alcohol [1].

Tobacco, alcohol, and immunosuppression (e.g. renal transplant patients, HIV) increase overall risk, and HPV type 16 and 18 infection is now recognised as an independent risk factor for oropharyngeal SCC [1].
problems.presentation:
The clinical picture the source describes:

- A **painless ulcer** with firm raised edges, an indurated, inflamed, granular base, and fixation to surrounding tissues [3]. Pain is usually a late feature [3].
- May present instead as a swelling, a white patch, an erythro-leucoplakia, or an erythroplakia [3].
- Malignancy should be suspected if any such lesion persists for **more than 3 weeks** [3].
- Lower lip vermilion is the classic site. Patient is typically male, sixth or seventh decade, outdoor worker.
- A cervical lymph node may be the presenting complaint if there is already metastatic spread [3].
problems.results:
- **Biopsy** is mandatory — this is the only way to confirm the diagnosis. Refer immediately via the urgent cancer pathway rather than waiting to see if the lesion resolves.
- Histology: SCC. Characteristically shows invasion of deep tissues with cellular pleomorphism and increased nuclear staining [4].
- Staging uses TNM classification. Prognosis for stage I (T1–N0) is >85% at 5 years; stage IV is around 10% [5]. Nodal involvement alone reduces cure rates by 50% [5].
- Presence or absence of extracapsular spread in metastatic cervical nodes is the most important single prognostic factor [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The critical distinction from benign lower lip lesions:

- **Duration >3 weeks**: any ulcer or white patch persisting beyond 3 weeks must be referred for biopsy [3]. This threshold exists because benign traumatic ulcers heal; SCC does not.
- **Induration**: the firm, fixed base and raised edges distinguish it from aphthous ulceration (soft, mobile, heals in 2 weeks) and mucocele (fluctuant, smooth, inner surface).
- **Actinic cheilitis** is the premalignant stage — blurred vermilion border, dry, scaled, white patches on the lower lip after years of UV exposure [2]. The transition from premalignant to malignant is the clinical worry.
- Unlike intraoral SCC where floor of mouth and lateral tongue are the highest-risk sites, lip SCC is dominated by sun exposure rather than tobacco/alcohol.
problems.treatment:
The goal is surgical excision, usually combined with radiotherapy for advanced disease.

- **Immediate urgent referral** via the two-week-wait cancer pathway. Do not wait, do not treat empirically.
- Management decisions are based on TNM stage and the patient's fitness for surgery [6].
- In many instances of oral cancer, combined surgery and radiotherapy constitutes optimal treatment [6].
- Pre-malignant actinic cheilitis: advise sun block and arrange regular follow-up [2]. If active intervention is indicated, laser excision or vermilionectomy are options.
- Stopping smoking is part of the treatment plan for any tobacco-related risk [1].
problems.prognosis:
- Stage I (T1–N0): >85% survival at 5 years [5].
- Stage IV: approximately 10% survival at 5 years [5].
- Nodal involvement reduces cure rates by 50% [5].
- Overall oral cancer mortality rate is just over 50% despite treatment [7]. Oral cancer is preventable in 75% of cases [7].
- Early diagnosis is the single biggest lever — the stage at presentation determines survival more than the treatment modality.

citations.quote: The main aetiological factor in cancer of the lip is exposure to sunlight, as with skin cancer. It is estimated that the risk of developing lip cancer doubles every 250 miles nearer the equator. Excessive alcohol and tobacco use are the important factors in the aetiology of cancer of the mouth showing a 'synergistic effect'. Perhaps the most clear-cut aetiological factor is the chewing of tobacco and paan. HPV type 16 and 18 infection is now recognized as an independent risk factor for oropharyngeal SCC. Immunosuppression, e.g. in renal transplant patients or patients with HIV, ↑ the risk of this and other tumours.
Sun damage to the lower lip causes excessive keratin production and ↑ mitotic activity in the basal layer. Premalignant. Advise sun blocks and regular follow-up.

Oral cancer is most often seen as a painless ulcer, although it may present as a swelling or as an area of leucoplakia, erythroleucoplakia, or erythroplakia. Patients may present with a history of a neck lump as a result of metastatic spread to cervical lymph nodes. Malignancy should be suspected if any of these lesions persists for >3 weeks. Pain is usually a late feature. Referred otalgia is a common manifestation of pain from the tongue or oropharyngeal cancer. The ulcer is described as firm with raised edges, with an indurated, inflamed, granular base and is fixed to surrounding tissues.

Mostly SCC. Characteristically shows invasion of deep tissues with cellular pleomorphism and ↑ nuclear staining. The presence of a lymphocytic response may have prognostic value, as does the manner of invasion (pushing or spreading). Can spread via local infiltration or lymphatic system (cervical nodes), and late spread via bloodstream.

This is dependent on site and stage,3 (prognosis for stage I is >85% and for stage IV is 10% over 5yrs), and co-morbidity. The presence or absence of extracapsular spread of tumour in metastatic cervical nodes is the most important single prognostic factor. Nodal involvement ↓ cure rates by 50%.

Various parameters affect the choice of Rx for patients with oral cancer; not least among these, but often forgotten, are the patients themselves, their general health, understanding of their disease, geographical location, and social and domestic commitments. Classically, broad Rx principles are based on tumour staging, using the Tumour, Node, Metastasis (TNM) classification, and the patient's fitness for surgery. In many instances of oral cancer, combined surgery and radiotherapy constitutes optimal Rx.

Cancer of the mouth (Fig. 11.4) accounts for ~2% of all malignant tumours in northern Europe and the US, but ~30–40% in the Indian subcontinent. >90% of these are SCCs. Globally it is the sixth commonest cause of cancer-related death. >2000 new cases of oral cancer are registered per year in the UK and each year half that number die from or with the disease. Oral cancer is preventable in 75% of cases. Overall mortality rate is just over 50% despite Rx.

problems.description: Dry, peeling, or cracked lips with no specific site. The patient habitually licks or picks at them. No blistering, no commissure involvement.
problems.conditionName: Cheilitis simplex (lip licker's dermatitis / dry sore lips)
problems.etiology:
The most common cause is a habit cycle: the lips feel dry, the patient licks them, the saliva evaporates and leaves them drier than before, so they lick again [1]. Wind exposure and sunlight cause direct drying of the vermilion, which has no sebaceous glands to maintain its moisture barrier. Viral illness can present this way too [1].

The reason the cycle perpetuates is mechanical: repeated wetting and drying of the vermilion disrupts the epithelium's barrier function. Skin around the mouth may show a faint ring of redness tracing the extent of the tongue's reach — the classic "licker's border".

This is distinguished from actinic cheilitis (which is premalignant, driven by UV, and shows keratotic changes) and exfoliative cheilitis (persistent crusting and scaling of unknown aetiology, more severe) by its self-sustaining habit aetiology and its benign, reversible course.
problems.presentation:
- Dry, cracked, peeling vermilion — often worse in winter or during illness.
- Mild soreness but no vesiculation, no ulceration, no gold crusting at the angles.
- In children and younger adults: a visible perioral ring of slight redness or hyperpigmentation tracing the licking habit.
- Patient often aware of the habit; may also report picking or peeling the dry skin.
- No systemic symptoms. No lymphadenopathy.
problems.results:
No investigations are routinely needed. This is a clinical diagnosis based on history and pattern.

- If the appearance is persistent, unusual, or associated with systemic features, consider:
  - **Patch testing** to exclude contact allergic cheilitis from toothpaste, lipstick, or food flavourings.
  - **FBC and haematinics** if there is also angular cheilitis or a burning tongue — haematinic deficiency contributes.
- The absence of vesicles, the absence of commissure involvement, and the licking history distinguish this from herpes labialis and angular cheilitis respectively.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key framing: **this is a habit-driven condition, not an infective one.**

- No vesicles (unlike herpes labialis), no commissure involvement (unlike angular cheilitis), no persistent crusting (unlike exfoliative cheilitis).
- The perioral ring of redness from licking is specific to this condition when present.
- Responds promptly to barrier treatment and habit interruption — that response itself helps confirm the diagnosis.
- Exfoliative cheilitis is sometimes described as similar to actinic cheilitis but of unknown aetiology [2]; it presents with more persistent, heavier crusting than simple dry lips and does not resolve with lip salve alone.
problems.treatment:
- **Lip salves** applied regularly — lanolin or petroleum jelly-based emollients restore the surface barrier [1]. The patient needs to understand why: salves replace the moisture barrier that licking destroys.
- Break the licking habit. Explain the cycle — the licking is the problem, not the solution.
- Protect against wind and sunlight with a lip balm containing SPF.
- If a contact allergen is suspected, identify and remove it (toothpaste flavouring, lipstick, nickel in instruments).
- Exfoliative cheilitis of unknown aetiology: manage symptomatically, consider topical steroids if inflamed, and refer if persistent.
problems.prognosis:
- With barrier treatment and habit interruption, simple dry lips resolve completely.
- Without habit change, the cycle continues indefinitely.
- Exfoliative cheilitis and actinic cheilitis carry a worse prognosis: actinic cheilitis is premalignant and requires follow-up [3]; exfoliative cheilitis is persistent and of unknown aetiology [2].

citations.quote: Except when accompanied by frank cheilitis, this is usually entirely innocent and can be treated symptomatically. Common causes are lip licking, and exposure to wind or sunlight. It is also a manifestation of viral illness. Rx: lip salves.
This is similar to actinic cheilitis but of unknown aetiology.
Sun damage to the lower lip causes excessive keratin production and ↑ mitotic activity in the basal layer. Premalignant. Advise sun blocks and regular follow-up.

problems.description: Firm, diffuse swelling of the lips that comes and goes but never fully resolves. No urticaria, no anaphylaxis. Younger patient, often with oral soreness or ulcers alongside.
problems.etiology:
A granulomatous inflammation of the lips, cheeks, or face — histologically identical to Crohn's disease, showing non-caseating granuloma on biopsy [1]. It may be:

- The initial or isolated manifestation of Crohn's disease.
- Related to sarcoidosis.
- A hypersensitivity response to benzoates (found in toothpaste) or other food additives such as tomatoes [1, 2].

The condition typically develops before the third decade of life [3]. The precise mechanism is unclear, but the granulomatous response suggests a dysregulated immune reaction — probably to a food or environmental antigen in genetically susceptible individuals [2].
problems.presentation:
What you'll typically see:

- **Diffuse lip swelling** that develops slowly, fluctuates, and persists — lasting days to weeks per episode, with incomplete resolution over time [3].
- The lips progressively firm up with repeated episodes, eventually becoming persistently swollen [3].
- Perioral skin may become red, dry, itchy, or cracked; angular cheilitis can develop [3].
- Oral soreness, mouth ulcers, and a cobblestone buccal mucosa are common accompanying features [3, 4].
- No urticaria, no systemic allergy features, no rapid-onset anaphylaxis — this distinguishes it from angioedema.
problems.results:
- **Biopsy of the lip or buccal mucosa**: the defining result. Non-caseating granuloma on histology is required to confirm the diagnosis [1].
- **Patch testing for allergens**: benzoates and other food additives [1].
- **Exclusion of systemic disease**: Crohn's and sarcoidosis must be ruled out before diagnosing isolated orofacial granulomatosis [2]. Investigations include CXR, serum ACE, calcium, and gastroenterology referral if bowel symptoms are present.
- The lip swelling of OFG is expected to last days to weeks before resolving; acute inflammatory causes such as angioedema resolve within 48 hours [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The useful contrasts:

- **Angioedema** (allergic or hereditary): rapid onset, resolves within 24–48 hours, may be triggered by a specific allergen or medication [5]. OFG is slower and more persistent.
- **Angular cheilitis**: confined to the commissures and infective in nature — OFG causes diffuse lip swelling and angular cheilitis can develop on top of it [3].
- **Crohn's disease**: OFG is histologically identical — the diagnosis of isolated OFG requires exclusion of systemic Crohn's [2].
- The cobblestone buccal mucosa and oral ulcers alongside the lip swelling are a helpful ensemble pointing to OFG rather than a purely labial condition.
problems.treatment:
Specific to the local problem:

- **Intralesional triamcinolone** injected into the affected lip — the first-line local treatment [1, 2]. 1 mL (40 mg) per injection under LA [6].
- Identify and avoid dietary allergens, particularly benzoates and tomatoes. Elimination diet guided by patch test results [1, 2].

problems.prognosis:
- The progression of OFG is unpredictable; patients need to be informed of this explicitly [7].
- Allergen avoidance combined with intralesional steroid can achieve significant improvement in many cases.
- In some patients, the lip swelling becomes permanently firm and disfiguring despite treatment.
- Systemic Crohn's, if present, follows its own course independently of the oral manifestations.

citations.quote: (Orofacial granulomatosis.) This is characterized by diffuse swelling of the lips, cheeks, or face and is histologically similar to Crohn's disease (non-caseating granuloma being found on biopsy). It may be the initial manifestation of Crohn's disease or related to sarcoidosis or completely isolated. It may be an allergic reaction to benzoates (toothpaste ingredient) or tomatoes. A patch test for allergens may be indicated. Intralesional steroids, e.g. triamcinolone into affected lip, anti-TNF therapies, or clofazimine 100–200mg daily for 3–6 months may help.

This is clinically and histologically identical to oral manifestations of Crohn's disease. ∆ of exclusion (Crohn's, sarcoid). Probable aetiology is as a hypersensitivity response to certain foods, additives such as benzoates, etc. ∆ is biopsy to demonstrate granulomata histologically and exclusion of systemic disease. Rx: specific to the local problem; e.g. lips (granulomatous cheilitis) intralesional steroid. Most beneficial Rx is to identify and avoid the irritant factors. Patients who have generalized Crohn's or very severe orofacial granulomatosis may benefit from systemic Rx with sulfasalazine or infliximab.

Given the patient's age, history and clinical findings, the most likely diagnosis is orofacial granulomatosis (OFG). This condition typically develops before the third decade of life and is thought to affect both genders equally. Lip swelling affects the majority of patients, with each episode lasting days to weeks. Over time, the lips may become firm and persistently swollen. The perioral skin may become red, dry, itchy or cracked, with some patients developing angular cheilitis.
The patient reports intermittent lip swelling and a sore mouth for the last 6 months.
The lip swelling of OFG would be expected to last days to weeks before resolving. Acute inflammatory causes such as angioedema resolve in 48 hours.
